newsitem.title: GERMANY: Greenpeace says EU approval for gene soya unsound.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace says EU approval for gene soya unsound.

text.p: The environmental group Greenpeace said on Wednesday the European Union's decision to approve imports of products derived from genetically-altered soybeans was based on incomplete information and was unsound.

It said data submitted to the EU by U.S. chemicals firm Monsanto were based on beans that had not been subjected to Monsanto's own "super weedkiller" Roundup, which the gene-altering process is intended to protect the plants against.
"As such the tests provide no information about the residue of this poison in the plants," Greenpeace's German campaign leader Joerg Naumann told a news conference in Frankfurt.
"EU approval must now be reversed," he said.
But Monsanto accused Greenpeace of "clutching at straws" and denied the charges.

"The safety analysis included tests on tolerant (genetically-altered) and non-tolerant beans that had been exposed to Roundup," said spokesman Tom McDermott at Monsanto's European headquarters in Brussels.
Soybeans are used in many food products ranging from baby milk to animal feed.

Greenpeace also said health safety tests carried out on the beans for EU approval had been insufficient and the risk of uncontrolled spread of the bean plants as a weed, particularly in frost-free zones, had not been thoroughly analysed.

McDermott also rejected this argument, saying: "The gene-altering process does not confer any hardiness on the plants. If there was a potential for that, soybean plants should be doing that now -- which they are not."
Greenpeace has had mixed results so far in its campaign against genetically-altered soybeans, which began entering Europe from the United States earlier this month.
Even in Germany, where the campaign has been strongest, most food manufacturers say they have no plans to boycott soyoil extracted from the altered beans.
However, Greenpeace has notched up successes with the German arms of Swiss food giant Nestle SA and Anglo-Dutch Unilever Plc/NV, which have agreed not to use the beans.
Greenpeace said it was still seeking to get the EU to overturn its approval of the soybeans, adding that an import ban was possible at the request of one EU member state.
It said it would be putting such a proposal to Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky in the coming weeks.
